trivia_fact: Observability was formally defined by Hungarian-American engineer Rudolf Kalman in 1960. In control theory, a system is observable if its internal state can be determined from its external outputs. Charity Majors and others popularized its application to software systems around 2017.

The "three pillars of observability" (logs, metrics, traces) became conventional wisdom, but Charity Majors and Ben Sigelman have argued this framing is misleading — it focuses on data types rather than the ability to ask arbitrary questions of your system without deploying new code.

OpenTelemetry was formed in 2019 by merging two competing CNCF projects: OpenCensus (backed by Google) and OpenTracing (backed by Uber/LightStep). The merge ended a confusing standards war and created the second-most-active CNCF project after Kubernetes.

Jaeger, Uber's open-source distributed tracing system, is named after the German word "Jager" meaning "hunter." The metaphor: tracing "hunts" requests across microservices. It was donated to CNCF in 2017 and graduated in 2019.

Zipkin was created at Twitter in 2012, inspired by Google's Dapper tracing paper. The name "Zipkin" comes from the B. J. Zipkin character — but is also a play on how traces "zip" across services following requests at speed.

Traditional logging produced unstructured text lines parsed with regex. Structured logging (emitting JSON or key-value pairs) gained momentum around 2015, making logs queryable without fragile parsing. Libraries like Go's zap and Python's structlog drove adoption.

High cardinality (many unique values for a dimension, like user IDs or request IDs) is essential for debugging but extremely expensive to store as metrics. This tension drove the development of columnar event stores like Honeycomb, which handle high-cardinality data natively.

Google published the Dapper paper in 2010, describing its production distributed tracing system. Dapper inspired virtually every open-source tracing system that followed: Zipkin, Jaeger, and eventually OpenTelemetry's trace model.

Service Level Objectives (SLOs) backed by error budgets were popularized by Google's SRE book. The insight: instead of targeting 100% uptime (impossible), define an acceptable error rate and "spend" the budget on shipping features. When the budget is exhausted, freeze deployments.

Honeycomb popularized "wide events" — single structured events with hundreds of fields capturing full request context. This approach contrasts with traditional metrics (pre-aggregated) and logs (unstructured text), enabling exploratory debugging without predefined dashboards.

W3C Trace Context became a standard in 2020, defining HTTP headers (traceparent, tracestate) for propagating trace context across services. Before this, every tracing system used incompatible headers, making cross-vendor tracing nearly impossible.

Flame graphs were invented by Brendan Gregg at Joyent in 2011 to visualize stack trace profiling data. The x-axis shows stack depth and the y-axis shows the call hierarchy. They became the standard visualization for CPU and memory profiling across all major platforms.
